definitions.meaning: first meaning: a stand-in, such as an actor's look-alike in risky scenes
second meaning: the word that can stand in front of each of those answers

explanation.walkthrough: Put the answer in front of each listed entry: double glazing, double-barrelled, double agent, double indemnity, double-jointed, double Scotch, double pneumonia, double-dealer.
explanation.definitionFit: A stunt stand-in on a film set is called a body double, and the same word prefixes every listed answer in phrases.

clue.text: Crash when taxi turns left into river

indicators.note: going into something means being placed inside it, so the earlier pieces sit within the river

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland and in Wales/England

indicators.note: something that turns faces the other way, so the vehicle word is read backwards

parts.note: a cab is a taxi
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A road accident: a taxi turns left and plunges into a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dee is a river in both Scotland and Wales, a crossword favourite; the reversed taxi and the L sit together inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A debacle is a sudden collapse or fiasco, a figurative smash-up, so it fits a crash in the sense of a complete failure.

parts.note: un is French for a
entry 13 is EPITAPH, and the classic epitaph is the abbreviation for 'rest in peace'

explanation.surface: Reads like an instruction to open a French document.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to 13-across, an epitaph, whose most familiar example on a gravestone is R.I.P.
explanation.definitionFit: To unrip is an old verb meaning to rip open or cut open, so it matches open as a verb.

clue.text: How hunters behave without hearts; one's in the right and one's inwhat?

indicators.note: one being in something means it is placed inside that word

parts.note: a lien is a legal right to hold property until a debt is paid
one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: without means lacking, and hearts is the card suit abbreviated, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: printed run together; 'in' signals insertion again and 'what' is taken as written
H is the card-playing abbreviation for hearts
one is the Roman numeral I again

explanation.surface: A riddling question about how hunters behave and who is in the right.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue splits into two halves, one for each word of the answer's tail; 'the right' is a legal right, not the political side. The printed 'inwhat' should read 'in what'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunters stalking prey stay hidden and still until it comes near, which is exactly what it means to ambush or lurk.

clue.text: Light fitting good for burning daylight

parts.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
burning daylight is wasting the day doing nothing, idling about

explanation.surface: Seems to be about an electric light fitting and wasting daylight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light fitting' suggests a lamp; it is the fitting of window glass that lets light in.
explanation.definitionFit: Glazing is the installing of glass panes in windows, a fitting that admits daylight into a building.

clue.text: Thought For The Day, say: "The Fate of the Olympians"

parts.note: the Olympians are the Greek gods of Mount Olympus
one's lot is one's fate

explanation.surface: Sounds like the title of a radio talk about the destiny of the Greek gods.
explanation.walkthrough: Thought for the Day is a short religious talk on BBC Radio 4's morning news programme. The Olympians' lot reads as GODS LOT.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcasting slot set aside for religious programmes is nicknamed this, and that BBC talk is an example.

clue.text: At the Turk's Head, in for another round, please!

parts.note: an aga was a Turkish commander or chief, a head
taken as written

explanation.surface: A drinker at a pub called the Turk's Head calls for another round.
explanation.walkthrough: The Turk's Head looks like a pub name; it is a Turkish head man, an aga.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling out the word as an exclamation asks for the same thing once more, like a refill of drinks.

parts.note: surface reading: the faces of people being sought by police
setter's reading: the picture of the face is put together from a kit of separate features

explanation.walkthrough: Police build a likeness of a wanted suspect from interchangeable eyes, noses and mouths supplied in a kit.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the trade name for a composite face assembled from stock features to show witnesses a suspect's likeness.

parts.note: surface reading: the cricketer stationed behind the stumps
setter's reading: a wicket is also a small gate, and the keeper of a gate confines people within it

explanation.walkthrough: At Oxford and Cambridge a student punished by being kept in college after hours is said to be gated; the cricket keeper is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means confining a student to college as a punishment, which is what a keeper of the gate would do.

parts.note: surface reading: a man named Bob is going downhill in life
setter's reading: a vehicle on runners, the second half of a bob racer, glides on skids over snow

explanation.walkthrough: Bob is the first half of bobsleigh, and the vehicle literally runs on skids.
explanation.definitionFit: A sledge pulled over snow rides on runners, or skids, and teamed with bob it names the racing sledge.

parts.note: a bar is the counter in a pub

indicators.note: to run counter is to go in the opposite direction, so the singer's name is read backwards

parts.note: Alfred Deller was a celebrated English countertenor

explanation.surface: A stuttering run of the same word, as if a countertenor's part were being counted.
explanation.walkthrough: Three counters, three jobs: a pub counter, a reversal signal, and the voice type identifying Alfred Deller.
explanation.definitionFit: To be barrelled is to be stored in barrels, which is to be held or contained in casks.

parts.note: an age is a long period of time
the clipped 'n' is just the letter N
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A tool used over and over, time and time again.
explanation.definitionFit: An agent can mean the means or instrument by which something is done, and a tool can be a person used by others.

parts.note: surface reading: poultry carved into thin pieces
setter's reading: a cockerel that has been cut, that is castrated, to fatten it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sliced' suggests carving at the table; the cut here was made to the live bird.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a castrated cockerel fattened for eating, so it is a bird that has had the knife.

clue.text: Hammer demonstrator's excessive claim to a London borough?

parts.note: a demonstrator of hammer-throwing would say of himself that he slings it
claiming to throw a ton is an exaggerated boast

explanation.surface: A hammer thrower boasts that he hurls a ton.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the borough as the thrower's boast: 'I sling (a) ton'.
explanation.definitionFit: Islington is an inner borough of north London, home to Arsenal football club.

indicators.note: stove is the past tense of stave, to smash in, so the following letters are broken up

parts.note: the hat's name splits after its first five letters, which act on the rest; the remainder is taken as written

explanation.surface: A last puff of smoke rising from a tall top hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stovepipe hat' reads as one item, but stove is split off to act on pipe hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A puff is a piece of flattering praise, and the last tribute paid to someone is inscribed on their gravestone.

clue.text: Bond: 'e's out of his tiny mind! On the contrary, not his, unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things gone awry, so the letters end up out of order

parts.note: 'e is he with its H dropped, the 'not his' of the clue
taken as written
turns 'out of' round to 'in', so the dropped-aitch pronoun joins the other letters rather than leaving them

explanation.surface: A put-down of James Bond as a man who has lost his little mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the contrary' turns 'out of' into 'in': E goes in with TINY MIND, and 'not his' notes that 'e has lost the H of he.
explanation.definitionFit: An indemnity is a security or guarantee against loss, and a bond is a binding pledge of that kind.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a ruling group of three people
second meaning: a Russian sledge drawn by three horses abreast across the frozen plains

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second meaning is described loosely: the vehicle runs over the snowy steppes rather than governing them.
explanation.definitionFit: The Russian word for a team of three horses is used for any group of three leaders sharing power.

clue.text: Miss Woodhouse left sadly for one raising the standard

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone badly, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: Emma Woodhouse is the heroine of Jane Austen's novel Emma
L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Jane Austen's heroine is left unhappy for the sake of someone raising standards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raising the standard' sounds like improving quality; the standard is a flag.
explanation.definitionFit: The oriflamme was the red banner of the early French kings, a flag carried into battle, so it is a standard.

clue.text: Scott's post: standing to in return journey

indicators.note: in places the little word inside the travel word
a return trip goes back the way it came, so the travel word is read backwards

parts.note: a ride is a journey
taken as written; standing means it stays upright, unreversed

explanation.surface: A note about Captain Scott's base camp on his return journey from the Pole.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott is not the polar explorer but C.P. Scott, the long-serving editor of the Manchester Guardian.
explanation.definitionFit: C.P. Scott held the top job at the Manchester Guardian for decades, so his post was in charge of the newspaper.

indicators.note: talk of means as spoken, so we want something that sounds like the following phrase

parts.note: Raleigh can be said 'Rally', and a lapse is a failure

explanation.surface: Recounting the fall of Sir Walter Raleigh, explorer and courtier.
explanation.walkthrough: Raleigh's name has several pronunciations, one close to 'rally'; run together with lapse it approximates the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverse is a setback, and falling back into illness or bad habits after improving is just such a setback.

parts.note: someone sharing a job holds it jointly
entry 17 is EDITOR, abbreviated as ED

explanation.surface: An eloquent person sharing an editing job.
explanation.walkthrough: A joint editor shares the job; 'Articulate' reads as eloquent but means having joints.
explanation.definitionFit: Articulate as an adjective in biology describes something made of segments linked by hinges, like a limb.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: hears a case in court and gives a verdict
second meaning: the book of the Bible that tells of the prophetess Deborah

explanation.walkthrough: Deborah was one of the leaders of Israel recorded in an Old Testament book named after them.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means tries in court, and the plural noun names the seventh book of the Old Testament.

clue.text: Literary giant in the cave of Trophonius

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the giant of Doubting Castle in Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress
second meaning: the Greek oracle cave whose visitors were said never to smile again

explanation.walkthrough: 'Literary giant' suggests a great author; it is a giant in a book. Trophonius's oracle left consultants in deep gloom.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopelessness is both the name of Bunyan's giant and the gloom said to haunt anyone who entered that oracle's cave.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to put a stop to a plan or rumour
second meaning: whisky distilled in Scotland

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests lacing a drink; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: To scotch a rumour is to kill it off, as an editor spikes a story, and the drink is Scottish whisky.

clue.text: Made love with one from model police force

indicators.note: force suggests violent rearrangement, so what remains is shaken into a new order
taking things from a group removes them, so these letters leave the phrase

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O
one is the Roman numeral I
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tabloid line about a romance within an exemplary police force.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove an O and an I from MODEL POLICE, then rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: If someone made you do something they forced or obliged you, and the past participle matches that past-tense sense.

clue.text: That's Gibson in there, up a gum tree

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards
in there places the actor inside the abbreviation just named

parts.note: i.e. abbreviates id est, that is
Mel Gibson is the actor

explanation.surface: Pointing out Mel Gibson stuck up a gum tree, an Aussie phrase for being in a fix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up a gum tree' is an Australian idiom for being in trouble, apt for the Australian-raised actor; here it is just the resin source.
explanation.definitionFit: Elemi is a fragrant resin from tropical trees used in varnishes, so it names a gum and the trees yielding it.

indicators.note: absorbing means taking something inside, so the circling word wraps round the numeral

parts.note: laps are circuits of a track
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A stone circle soaking something up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stone circles' reads as Stonehenge-type monuments, but the definition is just Stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapis, short for lapis lazuli, is a deep blue semiprecious mineral used in jewellery.

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument
Al Capp was the American cartoonist of Li'l Abner

explanation.surface: A harsh critic described as a writer of the Capp school.
explanation.definitionFit: Penal means punitive or severe, as in penal taxes or penal rates that show no mercy.

indicators.note: to dish is to ruin or wreck, so the preceding letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: the answer is a dish, and also what you might exclaim on hearing a petri dish called a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripe is the stomach lining of cattle cooked as a dish, and as an exclamation it dismisses something as rubbish.

clue.text: The old man's friend might take a breather

definitions.meaning: first meaning: William Osler's name for the illness that brings the aged a gentle death
second meaning: a lung disease that can carry off, or take, anyone who breathes

explanation.walkthrough: The physician William Osler called this lung infection 'the old man's friend' for the quiet death it brings.
explanation.definitionFit: This lung infection was the merciful killer of frail elderly patients, carrying off a breathing person.

parts.note: a rick is a stack of hay
a wire is a telegram

explanation.surface: A man named Rick sends a message that comes out garbled.
explanation.walkthrough: Rick looks like a name; it is a haystack.
explanation.definitionFit: Going haywire means going wildly wrong or out of control, so the word fits muddled or jumbled.

parts.note: surface reading: someone's hand held in another person's, as in a handshake
setter's reading: the cards a player holds are dealt out by one person at the table

explanation.walkthrough: A hand in cards is in the gift of whoever distributes the pack.
explanation.definitionFit: At the card table the person giving out the cards decides what each player holds.
